summary: Speculum is an interactive web tool for choosing where on Earth to test a rover, drill, habitat, or power system before it flies to the Moon or Mars. Its catalog has 89 locations: 23 backed by published analog literature and 66 candidates scored on climate alone, 61 of which came from a global climate scan of places outside the catalog. All sites are scored against lunar, Martian, and Europan targets. Users describe their project and get a ranked list that shows why each site scored as it did, how complete its data is, and where the analogy breaks down. All climate values come from 25 years of NASA POWER data, and the planetary reference values come from the NASA NSSDC Moon and Mars Fact Sheets.
details:
What it is

Speculum is a free web tool that helps teams choose where on Earth to field-test hardware meant for the Moon or Mars. Pick your project and your target world, and it ranks the best analog sites for you, with the uncertainty shown next to every result.

Try it: https://gpradines.github.io/speculum/

The problem

No place on Earth is truly like Mars or the Moon. Still, teams need somewhere realistic to test their rovers, drills, and habitats. The evidence is scattered across decades of papers, so teams often default to the same few famous sites without comparing alternatives.

What you can do with Speculum

  • Map: Explore documented analog sites and climate-only candidates. Each site has a panel with its climate values and confidence levels, its strengths and weaknesses, how testing there helps exploration, and access and permit warnings. A “where the analogy breaks down” section compares the site to the Moon or Mars in plain language (for example, how many times the site’s air pressure exceeds Mars’s).
  • Finder: Choose a project type (wheeled rover, ice drilling, habitat and ISRU, power and communications, and more), a target environment (lunar south pole, lunar lava tubes, equatorial Mars, Mars mid-latitudes with ice, and more), your logistics filters, and, if you want, your own parameter weights. You get the top 10 sites in two tiers: Tier A (backed by published analog studies) and Tier B (climate similarity only). Every result has a per-parameter breakdown, and you can export the list as CSV.
  • Methods: The full scoring method, a worked example, all 29 parameters, confidence rules, known limitations, and the complete source list.

How the ranking works

  • Ranking is relative: Nowhere on Earth reaches the real cold, thin air, or dryness of Mars or the Moon. So each target defines a direction (equatorial Mars, for example, is colder, drier, and thinner-aired than most of Earth), and each site is scored by its percentile position along that direction among all sites.
  • Weights depend on the project: A drilling project cares most about ground ice and cold; a rover cares about terrain and dryness. Weights are scaled by how reliable the data is, and you can adjust them.
  • Only real data is scored: Of the 29 parameters in our schema, 12 currently have data. Each result states its coverage (for example, “based on 7 of 12 parameters with data”) and shows low-confidence warnings. The remaining parameters (slope, rock abundance, soil bearing strength, radiation, and others) are listed openly as future work.
  • Priorities are set: When a published paper and NASA POWER disagree on a parameter, the paper wins. Where the coarse grid clearly misrepresents a mountain or island site, we removed the grid values instead of keeping misleading numbers.

Looking beyond the usual suspects

To find places the literature hasn’t covered, we scanned 64 regions that are not in our catalog, including the Gobi, Taklamakan, Pamir, Altiplano, the Antarctic and Greenland ice domes, and Kamchatka. This surfaced candidates such as the Pamir Plateau and Altun Shan for equatorial Mars rovers, and Dome A and Axel Heiberg for the lunar south pole. These are clearly labeled as hypotheses based on climate data only, with no literature behind them yet.

Does it work?

As a sanity check, Speculum ranks well-known analogs where experts would expect them: Concordia for ice and cold, Atacama for astrobiology. We also built reference test cases with expected rankings and compared the tool’s output against them. For a wheeled rover on equatorial Mars, the results were Qaidam 74.0, MDRS 67.7, Death Valley 60.1, and Atacama 54.2.

Where the analogy fails

We want to be upfront about the limits:

  • Earth analogs never reproduce reduced gravity, lunar vacuum, the Martian atmosphere, or the radiation environment.
  • Concordia ranks high for ice and cold, but it is really an analog for isolation and extreme cold, and says little about terrain.
  • Climate-only candidates have low confidence and need local verification before any real test campaign.
  • Many coordinates are approximate.

Why it matters

Speculum turns scattered analog knowledge into one transparent ranking tool, and it never hides how uncertain the answer is. Its discovery scan also points to less-studied regions that deserve a closer look.

What’s next

  • A continuous global grid scan instead of hand-picked regions
  • Slope and roughness from elevation data (NASA and other agencies)
  • Ice and permafrost layers
  • Verification with local field stations
  • More Europa and lunar-polar analogs
